summary: Defines a Telnet option for checking the round-trip path between two Telnet modules. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The Telnet Timing Mark option lets one end check whether earlier data has passed through the other end's buffers. This helps a program decide which buffered input or output to discard before continuing.

subtitle: A Telnet marker helps two ends identify when earlier data has passed through a connection.

tldr.problem: A Telnet user or process may need to know when earlier data has reached the other end, especially when clearing buffered input or output.
tldr.mechanism: One side requests a TIMING-MARK. The other places a reply marker at the agreed point in its data flow and returns WILL TIMING-MARK after the marker passes through its buffers.
tldr.outcome: The option can help measure delay or synchronize an interaction. By default, neither end attempts this synchronization.

today: RFC 860 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. The metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a Timing Mark Helps
sections.content:
The option addresses a common problem in an interactive Telnet session: data can wait in buffers at either end. A process may want to know when earlier input has reached the other side before it resumes handling later input.

For example, after an invalid command, a server can ask the user's system to return a timing mark. The server can discard unwanted type-ahead until the mark shows where the user's input stream has progressed.
sections.plainLanguage: A program may need to know when earlier characters have passed through a Telnet connection. The timing mark gives both ends a point to use when deciding what data to keep or discard.

sections.title: Requesting the Option
sections.content:
The option's command name is TIMING-MARK, with code 6. A sender uses IAC DO TIMING-MARK to request that the receiver return WILL TIMING-MARK at the appropriate point in the stream.

The receiver can refuse with WON'T TIMING-MARK. The default is WON'T and DON'T, so the two ends do not explicitly try to synchronize unless they negotiate the option.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks for a timing mark, and the other can agree or refuse. If neither side negotiates the option, they make no special attempt to synchronize.

sections.title: Where the Reply Is Placed
sections.content:
When the receiver agrees, it lets the requested mark pass through its outgoing buffer, then routes the mark into its incoming buffer toward the requester. Once the mark has passed through that incoming buffer, the receiver sends WILL TIMING-MARK.

When the requester receives that reply, it knows that data it sent before the request has been delivered to the other host. The reply also marks progress for data that the other host sent before the mark turned around.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is sent after the mark passes through the other end's buffers. Receiving it tells the requester that earlier data has moved through the connection to that point.

sections.title: Uses and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC lists measuring round-trip delay, clearing unwanted type-ahead, and clearing unwanted output as typical uses. A process can read and discard data until it receives the timing mark, then resume normal handling.

The mark helps identify the boundary of unwanted data; it does not itself discard characters. The system that requested the mark remains responsible for throwing away any data it no longer wants.
sections.plainLanguage: A program can use the mark to measure delay or find where to stop discarding data. The program must still decide which data to throw away.
